articles.title: Inside Health - Where are we at with long Covid? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Millions of people still have long Covid, yet a cure still isn't quite within reach.
articles.body: More than six years since the start of the Covid pandemic, it might feel like we're pretty over it, yet that's simply not the case for the millions of people who suffer from long Covid. But could there be hope on the horizon? A new clinical trial led by University College London and University College London Hospitals found that over-the-counter antihistamines and a prescription anti-inflammatory drug called colchicine offered a small reduction in fatigue for people with long Covid. But it's still not a cure. Professor Danny Altmann, an immunologist at Imperial College London, joins us to discuss this new research and the problems with understanding long Covid. He also tells us about some of the upcoming studies that might help us better get a handle on the condition. Also this week, did you know that around one in 335 people in the UK are living with a stoma? Yet according to Colostomy UK, more than 60 per cent of those with a stoma say a lack of suitable toilet facilities affects their daily lives. Thanks to a campaign that started in Bristol, B&Q has now made the disabled toilets across its stores stoma-friendly. We pay a visit to B&Q with The Traitors' Mollie Pearce, who has been living with a stoma since she was 18, and colorectal surgeon Ms Caroline Burt from Bristol Foundation Trust to find out more. Finally, many of us have been guzzling ice cream to cool off during the hot weather. But have you seen the social media claims that the frozen treat can reduce your risk of developing type 2 diabetes? We asked nutritional scientist Dr Sarah Berry from King's College London to give us the scoop on the 'ice cream paradox'. Presenter: James Gallagher Producer: Alice Lipscombe-Southwell Production coordinator: Stu Laws Editor: Ilan Goodman

articles.title: 'Scared to death': Thousands evacuate Nevada homes as wildfire spreads
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people in the US state have been warned to evacuate as the wildfire spreads in the outskirts of Reno.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people in the US state of Nevada have been told to evacuate their homes as a wildfire approached the city of Reno.

Eyewitnesses recorded videos showing the blaze and plumes of smoke in the outskirts of the city as the fire continued to spread over the weekend.

Six people have been injured, according to local authorities, with windy and unpredictable weather contributing to the fire's spread.

articles.title: Inside Health - A new era for type 1 diabetes treatment - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Plus, how much do people really change their habits for a free coffee?
articles.body: Insulin has been used to treat type 1 diabetes for more than a century but now there is a new treatment being rolled out on the NHS that can delay the onset of the disease for years. Alongside, screening is gathering pace, identifying those that could benefit. So, is this the beginning of a new era for type 1 diabetes treatment? Dima and his mum Elena explain what it was like to be told that he had tested positive for developing type 1 diabetes and what it was like taking part in the trial for this new drug, teplizumab. Parth Narendran, a Professor of Diabetes Medicine at the University of Birmingham, and Consultant Paediatric Endocrinologist Dr Renuka Dias at Birmingham Women's and Children's Hospital, reveal how these changes are transforming treatment. In July, the NHS announced plans to incentivise us to walk a marathon a month by offering vouchers and discounts. But with scant detail on how the plan will actually work, we ask Joan Costa-i-Font, Professor of Health Economics at London School of Economics, what makes schemes like this succeed or fail. Plus, why are horse fly bites so painful? Dr Erica McAlister, an entomologist at the Natural History Museum, explains how the flies break into our skin, while consultant dermatologist Dr Alexandra Banner describes what’s happening in our bodies. Presenter: James Gallagher Producer: Hannah Robins

articles.title: Map: Track measles outbreaks, cases and vaccination rates by state across the U.S.
articles.summary: NBC News is tracking confirmed measles case counts and state infection tallies. This data will be updated regularly.
articles.body: Measles, one of the most contagious viruses in the world, is regularly infecting people in the U.S. again. Already in 2026 more than 2,700 cases have been counted, making 2026 the worst year for measles infections in the U.S. since the early 1990s. NBC News is continuing to track confirmed measles cases across the United States, using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Measles case counts reached a 34-year high last year, and eight months into 2026, this year’s total is even higher. The disease epicenter at the start of the year was in South Carolina, where the CDC has confirmed 600-plus measles cases. State officials declared the South Carolina outbreak over in April. Now, cases are surging in Pennsylvania, which has reported hundreds of new measles cases since July. The map below will be updated regularly to show year-to-date new measles case counts reported in each state and Washington, D.C. Measles infection counts skyrocketed last year with 2,289 confirmed cases, which had been the most reported since 1991. This comes despite the virus being marked as being “eliminated” in the U.S. —a designation meaning it is no longer constantly circulating — in 2000. The U.S. is in danger of losing that status following a year of continuous spread of the disease. Three people, including two young girls, died in the U.S. from measles last year. The major outbreaks last year began with West Texas in February. In October, a measles outbreak occurred along the Utah and Arizona border. In all, the CDC recorded 48 measles outbreaks in 2025, up from 16 in 2024. So far in 2026, 36 measles outbreaks have been reported. Childhood vaccination rates have been backsliding, leaving communities vulnerable to this deadly disease. The measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, marking a turning point for the contagious disease, which used to infect hundreds of thousands and kill thousands in the country every year. CORRECTION (Feb. 20, 2026, 3:57 p.m. ET): A previous version of a graphic in this article miscalculated the relative size of this year's measles case count. As of Feb. 20, this year's case count is four times the size of 2025's at the same point in the year, and 25 times the size of 2024's at the same point, not seven times and 30 times higher.

articles.title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicularâs viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
articles.summary: US Streamers News: The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It i.
articles.body: The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. It quietly brings attention to something that a lot of people who use the internet notice but don't often say out loud. People in different communities often have a bigger impact on each other than they think.Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trendsThe conversation begins with a confident and lighthearted comment from one of the trans women present. She says, "You know that trans women are like the OG lip masters, right? We are very talented in the program. Like, I do the peptides, I'm on Zeta." Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle. He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." Itâs not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.

articles.title: âThree-against-one situationâ: El Rubius opens up on being âtargetedâ in MrBeastâs viral $1M challenge
articles.summary: US Streamers News: El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeastâs $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a .
articles.body: El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeastâs $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.El Rubius reflects on a tough and âunfairâ exitSpeaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which Iâve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "Iâm happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough. I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. I kept trying to go after RaKai, but, well, he actually just got eliminated in the end. So, at least justice was served for Abraham. Abraham, if youâre watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, Iâm being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Seriously, thank you for all the support and for just being there."He added, "Every time I asked for something in the chat or whatever it was, you guys were right there. Youâre incredible. Iâm a little disappointed in myself, personally, mostly for not performing better, but hey, I gave it my all, and we still walked away with $50,000, so weâve got to look on the bright side. All right, guys, big hugs to all my brothers out there!"Interestingly, the story did not end with frustration. Later that day, Rubius revealed that MrBeastâs team had sent him a cake after his exit. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubiusâ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.

Choosing the best mortgage lender: What to know as a homebuyer

Your effort to find the best mortgage lender begins early in the home-buying process — before you start seriously shopping for a house.

You'll reach out to a lender to get an idea of where you stand. Perhaps confirm your homebuying qualifications with a second lender. Get a preapproval from one or the other. Then start house hunting.

After you have a contract on a home in hand, you'll expand your mortgage lender search, ask for loan offers, and narrow the field to a home loan lender that hits all the right notes.

You will also want to consider lenders that specialize in the type of loan you may be looking for (if you know) — that might include conventional loans, VA-backed mortgages, lenders that cater to first-time home buyers, FHA loans, refi, jumbo, or home equity products.

When shopping multiple lenders, protect your credit score by submitting all loan applications within 45 days. FICO considers numerous credit inquiries for a single type of loan within a 45-day period to be related and won't compound the impact to your credit score.

Types of mortgages offered by the best mortgage lenders

There are many types of mortgage loans, but the best mortgage lenders usually offer the following common kinds of home loans that benefit the most borrowers:

You might think of a conventional loan as a "regular mortgage." There are two types of conventional loans: conforming and jumbo. People often use the terms "conventional" and "conforming" interchangeably — a conforming loan is simply a mortgage under the limit set by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). A jumbo loan is a type of conventional loan for more than the FHFA limit, and you'll usually need a higher credit score and down payment to qualify.

FHA loans are mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). Though the FHA backs these mortgages, you'll still apply for them with a private mortgage lender. These are good options for first-time home buyers because they only require a 580 credit score (with a 3.5% down payment) or a 500 score (with a 10% down payment). You can also qualify with a higher debt-to-income ratio than with conventional loans.

A VA loan is insured by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and it's for people affiliated with the military and their spouses. VA loans don't have a set minimum credit score — the required score varies by lender. These loans also don't require a down payment.

Learn more: How to qualify for a VA loan

The list of mortgage types goes on and on, but here are a few other kinds of mortgage loans you might qualify for:

USDA loan : This mortgage is for low-income borrowers buying in qualifying rural areas, and it's insured by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Fixed-rate mortgage : This is a very common type of mortgage (you can get conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA loans with fixed rates) that keeps your rate the same for the entire life of the loan. On a 30-year loan, your monthly payment toward the mortgage principal and interest will be the same for the entire 30 years.

Adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) : An ARM locks in your rate for a predetermined amount of time and then changes it regularly. For example, a 5/1 ARM keeps your rate the same for the first five years, then it increases or decreases once a year for the rest of your term.

HELOCs and home equity loans : Home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans are "second mortgages." You borrow against the equity in your home and have a second mortgage payment along with your first one.

First, narrow your search down to three or four lenders. Apply for mortgage preapproval with all of them in a short timeframe so that when you're looking at interest rates and fees, you're comparing apples to apples. Once you have a preapproval letter in hand, you can start shopping for homes.

When you make an offer on a home — and it is accepted — you'll choose your favorite lender from your list and send them the necessary documentation, such as bank statements and tax returns, to apply for an official mortgage approval. The lender will usually take around 30 to 45 days to complete the underwriting process and schedule a closing day. The day you close on the house , you will sign the paperwork for your mortgage, become a homeowner, and receive the keys to your new house.

Top 5 characteristics of the best mortgage lenders

When adding lenders to your roster of contenders, look for these five traits shared by the best mortgage lenders:

A preapproval is the ticket to shopping for a house. But it's only the first step. The lenders competing to win your business should have low-friction application procedures and easy document exchange, preferably with secure online paperwork capabilities.

Starting out, you may not know your best loan option. Is it a conventional mortgage or an FHA-backed loan? Maybe a jumbo? The lenders you talk to should be well-equipped to meet your funding needs with a variety of mortgage loan types.

The best mortgage lenders fairly price their loans without piling on a lot of expensive fees. There is a long list of potential loan charges to be aware of, but a mortgage origination fee can be as much as 0.50% to 1% or more of the loan cost. Look for lenders who waive lender origination fees.

The best lenders will show interest rates on a number of loan options and clearly disclose fees built into the interest rate, such as discount points .

5. Responsive and proactive customer support

Are your questions answered quickly, and are you guided through the loan process along the way? The best mortgage lenders provide concierge-level service.

Yahoo Finance evaluated mortgage lenders using a data-driven scoring model combined with editorial analysis to identify the best options for a wide range of borrowers.

Our review is primarily based on 2025 Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data, focusing on the 100 largest mortgage lenders by loan volume. To ensure broad consumer relevance, we excluded credit unions without a national presence and open field of membership.

Each lender was scored across key categories:

Interest rates: Using 2025 HMDA data, we compared lenders based on how their issued mortgage rates stacked up against the annual median across reporting institutions. Lenders with a higher share of below-median rates received stronger scores.

Loan costs: We analyzed total loan costs using HMDA data and compared them to the national median, rewarding lenders that consistently offered more competitive overall borrowing costs.

Customer experience: We incorporated third-party data, including J.D. Power customer satisfaction rankings and Trustpilot reviews, along with an evaluation of customer support channels and availability.

Digital experience: We reviewed whether borrowers can complete key steps online — namely, applying for mortgage preapproval and/or mortgage loans.

After scoring lenders across these categories, our editorial team identified the highest-performing institutions and selected the final list of the 10 best mortgage lenders. Final selections were based not only on overall scores, but also on standout features, specialized loan offerings, or unique strengths that made each lender particularly well-suited for specific borrower needs.

The information in this article has not been reviewed or approved by any advertiser. The details on financial products, including interest rates and fees, are accurate as of the publish date. All products or services are presented without warranty. Check the lender's website for the most current information. This site doesn't include all currently available offers.

Mortgage lenders are often better than banks because they specialize in home loans rather than a variety of financial products. They also usually have a quicker mortgage underwriting process. But your bank could be a good fit if it offers special mortgage perks such as interest rate discounts for existing customers. Some national banks, such as Truist, also have the bandwidth to offer unique benefits to mortgage borrowers.

The best bank for you depends on factors like your credit score, down payment, and loan type. Getting quotes from multiple lenders lets you compare rates and fees side by side. According to analysis by Yahoo Finance, the top lenders to consider include Rocket Mortgage, Veterans United, Fifth Third Bank, loanDepot.com, Bank of America, Alliant Credit Union, Mutual of Omaha, Better, New American Funding, and AmeriSave.

Rocket Mortgage has been the nation's top mortgage lender by loan volume for several years. United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) has also held the top spot in certain periods, particularly among wholesale lenders. Ranking can shift year to year, so it's worth checking the most recent Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data for current figures.

The best place to get a mortgage depends on your priorities. Online lenders offer convenience and competitive rates, while credit unions often provide lower fees and personalized service to members. Banks can be advantageous if you already have accounts with them. A mortgage broker can shop multiple lenders on your behalf to find the most favorable terms.

No single lender consistently offers the lowest mortgage rates — rates vary based on your credit score, loan type, down payment size, and broader market conditions. Credit unions, online lenders, and community banks sometimes offer rates below those of large national banks. The best approach is to get quotes from at least three to five lenders and compare the annual percentage rate (APR), which includes fees alongside the interest rate.

A VA loan is insured by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and it's for people affiliated with the military and their spouses. VA loans don't have a set minimum credit score — the required score varies by lender. These loans also don't require a down payment.
Learn more: How to qualify for a VA loan
The list of mortgage types goes on and on, but here are a few other kinds of mortgage loans you might qualify for:
USDA loan : This mortgage is for low-income borrowers buying in qualifying rural areas, and it's insured by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Fixed-rate mortgage : This is a very common type of mortgage (you can get conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA loans with fixed rates) that keeps your rate the same for the entire life of the loan. On a 30-year loan, your monthly payment toward the mortgage principal and interest will be the same for the entire 30 years.

Adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) : An ARM locks in your rate for a predetermined amount of time and then changes it regularly. For example, a 5/1 ARM keeps your rate the same for the first five years, then it increases or decreases once a year for the rest of your term.

HELOCs and home equity loans : Home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans are "second mortgages." You borrow against the equity in your home and have a second mortgage payment along with your first one.

First, narrow your search down to three or four lenders. Apply for mortgage preapproval with all of them in a short timeframe so that when you're looking at interest rates and fees, you're comparing apples to apples. Once you have a preapproval letter in hand, you can start shopping for homes.

When you make an offer on a home — and it is accepted — you'll choose your favorite lender from your list and send them the necessary documentation, such as bank statements and tax returns, to apply for an official mortgage approval. The lender will usually take around 30 to 45 days to complete the underwriting process and schedule a closing day. The day you close on the house , you will sign the paperwork for your mortgage, become a homeowner, and receive the keys to your new house.
Top 5 characteristics of the best mortgage lenders
When adding lenders to your roster of contenders, look for these five traits shared by the best mortgage lenders:

A preapproval is the ticket to shopping for a house. But it's only the first step. The lenders competing to win your business should have low-friction application procedures and easy document exchange, preferably with secure online paperwork capabilities.

Starting out, you may not know your best loan option. Is it a conventional mortgage or an FHA-backed loan? Maybe a jumbo? The lenders you talk to should be well-equipped to meet your funding needs with a variety of mortgage loan types.

The best mortgage lenders fairly price their loans without piling on a lot of expensive fees. There is a long list of potential loan charges to be aware of, but a mortgage origination fee can be as much as 0.50% to 1% or more of the loan cost. Look for lenders who waive lender origination fees.
The best lenders will show interest rates on a number of loan options and clearly disclose fees built into the interest rate, such as discount points .
5. Responsive and proactive customer support
Are your questions answered quickly, and are you guided through the loan process along the way? The best mortgage lenders provide concierge-level service.
Yahoo Finance evaluated mortgage lenders using a data-driven scoring model combined with editorial analysis to identify the best options for a wide range of borrowers.

Our review is primarily based on 2025 Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data, focusing on the 100 largest mortgage lenders by loan volume. To ensure broad consumer relevance, we excluded credit unions without a national presence and open field of membership.
Each lender was scored across key categories:

Interest rates: Using 2025 HMDA data, we compared lenders based on how their issued mortgage rates stacked up against the annual median across reporting institutions. Lenders with a higher share of below-median rates received stronger scores.
Loan costs: We analyzed total loan costs using HMDA data and compared them to the national median, rewarding lenders that consistently offered more competitive overall borrowing costs.

Customer experience: We incorporated third-party data, including J.D. Power customer satisfaction rankings and Trustpilot reviews, along with an evaluation of customer support channels and availability.
Digital experience: We reviewed whether borrowers can complete key steps online — namely, applying for mortgage preapproval and/or mortgage loans.

After scoring lenders across these categories, our editorial team identified the highest-performing institutions and selected the final list of the 10 best mortgage lenders. Final selections were based not only on overall scores, but also on standout features, specialized loan offerings, or unique strengths that made each lender particularly well-suited for specific borrower needs.

The information in this article has not been reviewed or approved by any advertiser. The details on financial products, including interest rates and fees, are accurate as of the publish date. All products or services are presented without warranty. Check the lender's website for the most current information. This site doesn't include all currently available offers.

Mortgage lenders are often better than banks because they specialize in home loans rather than a variety of financial products. They also usually have a quicker mortgage underwriting process. But your bank could be a good fit if it offers special mortgage perks such as interest rate discounts for existing customers. Some national banks, such as Truist, also have the bandwidth to offer unique benefits to mortgage borrowers.

The best bank for you depends on factors like your credit score, down payment, and loan type. Getting quotes from multiple lenders lets you compare rates and fees side by side. According to analysis by Yahoo Finance, the top lenders to consider include Rocket Mortgage, Veterans United, Fifth Third Bank, loanDepot.com, Bank of America, Alliant Credit Union, Mutual of Omaha, Better, New American Funding, and AmeriSave.

Rocket Mortgage has been the nation's top mortgage lender by loan volume for several years. United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) has also held the top spot in certain periods, particularly among wholesale lenders. Ranking can shift year to year, so it's worth checking the most recent Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data for current figures.

The best place to get a mortgage depends on your priorities. Online lenders offer convenience and competitive rates, while credit unions often provide lower fees and personalized service to members. Banks can be advantageous if you already have accounts with them. A mortgage broker can shop multiple lenders on your behalf to find the most favorable terms.

No single lender consistently offers the lowest mortgage rates — rates vary based on your credit score, loan type, down payment size, and broader market conditions. Credit unions, online lenders, and community banks sometimes offer rates below those of large national banks. The best approach is to get quotes from at least three to five lenders and compare the annual percentage rate (APR), which includes fees alongside the interest rate.

articles.title: Louisiana warns against flesh-eating bacteria after five deaths
articles.summary: Louisiana health officials are urging residents to take precautions against a flesh-eating bacterial infection following the deaths of five people this year.
articles.body: Louisiana health officials are urging residents to take precautions against a flesh-eating bacterial infection following the deaths of five people this year. The Louisiana Department of Health issued a warning about the infection, known as Vibrio vulnificus, in a press release on Thursday. The department said nine people have been infected this year and five have died. By comparison, Louisiana averaged seven cases and one death annually over the previous 10 years during the same time period. All of this year’s reported cases were linked to wounds exposed to seawater, and all patients had underlying health conditions, the department added. Vibrio bacteria naturally live in coastal waters, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and is more common in the summer when water temperatures rise. People can contract the infection by eating raw or undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters, or when an open wound comes into contact with coastal waters, the CDC says. About 1 in 5 people with a Vibrio vulnificus infection die, according to the agency. While anyone can be infected, the Louisiana Department of Health said those most at risk include people with liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV or thalassemia; people undergoing immune-suppressing treatment; people taking medication that reduces stomach acid; and people who recently had stomach surgery. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever and chills, according to the CDC. The department urged residents to seek medical care immediately if a wound exposed to brackish or salt water becomes red, swollen, painful, warm or discolored, and to tell their health care provider about the water exposure. Louisiana saw a similar spike in Vibrio infection last year, with at least 17 cases were reported in the state. At least 10 people in Florida, Louisiana and the Outer Banks of North Carolina died from the infection last year, according to health officials.

articles.title: Why former NBA players say they’re drafting to the WNBA | CNN
articles.summary: Former NBA players Royce White and Enes Kanter Freedom declared “eligibility” for the WNBA in protest of the league’s transgender policies. CNN’s Ben Hunte explains why they’re doing this, as advocates and the WNBA players’ association responded by emphasizing inclusion and opposing hate toward transgender people.
articles.body:
Former NBA players Royce White and Enes Kanter Freedom declared “eligibility” for the WNBA in protest of the league’s transgender policies. CNN’s Ben Hunte explains why they’re doing this, as advocates and the WNBA players’ association responded by emphasizing inclusion and opposing hate toward transgender people.

articles.title: The week in 30 photos
articles.summary: Take a look at 30 photos of the week from August 6 to August 13.
articles.body: Emergency teams in Colombia have been desperately searching for survivors after the country experienced its worst earthquake in decades on Monday.At least 273 people were killed in the 7.4 magnitude quake, which damaged homes, schools, bridges and airports across a large swathe of the country. Hundreds of people still remained missing as of Thursday.The epicenter of the quake was in San José del Palmar, about 240 kilometers (149 miles) west of the capital city of Bogotá. Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella — who only took office last week — declared a state of national disaster to mobilize extra resources to the most affected regions.Here are some of the stories that made headlines over the past week, as well as some photos that caught our eye.

Now that a Supreme Court decision has cleared the way for the end of their deportation protections, advocates say many Haitians have been required to wear the ankle monitors. “It’s so humiliating,” says Vilès Dorsainvil of the Haitian Community Help and Support Center, one of the men comforting Maler in this photo. (Carol Guzy)Haitian immigrant Monsanto Maler became emotional and collapsed after receiving an ankle monitor at a Department of Homeland Security field office during a mandatory check in after thousands of Haitians lost Temporary Protected Status (TPS) during US President Trump’s controversial mass deportation effort in Blue Ash Ohio on August 9, 2026. He has lived in the US since 2023, saying he left Haiti because he didn’t feel safe. Haitians are fearful of an impending ICE immigration enforcement surge and being returned to their country which is still in the grip of anarchy and dangerous gang violence.

articles.title: Colombia’s earthquake tore apart this family with triplets. Only one survived
articles.summary: Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family.
articles.body: Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family. When the 7.4 magnitude earthquake shook western Colombia on August 10, the Saavedra Caycedo family was in their apartment in Cali, one of the hardest-hit cities. Search and rescue efforts at the site began immediately and continued for days. Family and friends took to the streets to ask for help and volunteer in the rescue operations. The triplets, Ana Maria, Sofia and Isabella Saavedra Caycedo; their father Jair Saavedra; their mother Vicky Caycedo and their uncle Diego Caycedo would all be pulled from the debris in the hours and days that followed. The parents were found embracing in their final moments. Sofia and Diego were found dead too. And Isabella’s body was the last to be pulled from the rubble, the triplets’ cousin Camila Martínez Sierra said. A family-organized GoFundMe campaign for Ana Maria has already received thousands of donations. The campaign page says she has already undergone surgery “and now faces a long recovery process.” “Our hearts are broken by the loss of my uncle Jairo and Vicky and my cousins Sofía and Isabella,” Marinez Sierra posted to Instagram on Friday. “Now is the time to stay united and be there for our cousin Ana. Every bit of help, prayer, donation, and sharing counts.” The triplets, according to the family’s fundraising campaign, had recently graduated from university and worked together. “They had dreams, plans, and a whole life ahead of them,” their family wrote on the GoFundMe page. “We want Ana María to have a solid foundation to recover physically and emotionally and to restart her life, without also having to worry about how to pay for everything that is to come.” Martínez Sierra remembered her relatives with several photos and videos of large family gatherings, trips, parties and moments they shared together. One photo shows the family dressed in matching white outfits and black hats, sitting poolside with wide smiles at what appears to be a family reunion. Another shows them gathered around a night-time bonfire. “I can only look at these videos and photos with a heart full of memories and a mix of love, nostalgia, and a pain I still don’t know how to explain,” she wrote in an Instagram post. “Here are our reunions, the laughter, the hugs, the family moments, my uncles, the triplets … moments we lived without imagining that one day we would look at these images in such a different way,” Martínez Sierra said. The Saavedra Caycedo family are among the at least 294 people confirmed to have been killed. Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management said another 320 are missing while nearly 4,000 were injured in the earthquake. More than 12,000 homes have been destroyed and over 100 buildings have been leveled. The earthquake was the deadliest to hit Colombia in decades. Families have been sharing urgent pleas on social media, hoping to track down missing loved ones and rescuers are continuing to work through the rubble. “One never thinks that a photo can become such a precious memory, nor that a hug that seemed so ordinary could become something we would keep forever in our hearts,” Martínez Sierra said. “This earthquake changed our lives in a matter of seconds,” Martínez Sierra said. “It reminded us, in the most painful way, that nothing is guaranteed and that many times we put off a hug, a phone call, an ‘I love you,’ a meeting, a visit.”

articles.title: 47-year-old California pastor makes college football comeback decades after injury stifled career
articles.summary: Justin Buzzard, a 47-year-old California pastor, joined San Jose City College as a defensive end after an injury ended his career decades ago.
articles.body: Nearly three decades after an injury cut his college football career short, a 47-year-old California pastor is putting the pads back on for an unlikely second shot at his on-field dream. "No one's going easy on me... and I'm not going easy on them," Justin Buzzard told "Fox & Friends First" co-host Todd Piro. "I'm giving them everything I've got, too." Buzzard, who recently made the San Jose City College Jaguars, said his much younger teammates have embraced him despite his initial uncertainty over how they would react to a 47-year-old joining the roster. RAVENS ARE SIGNING A 40-YEAR-OLD DEFENSIVE LINEMAN TO PLAY HIS 19TH NFL SEASON AND IT IS AWESOME "I was really wondering, 'How are they going to handle... a 47-year-old guy showing up?' Are they going to receive me? Are they going to accept me? Will they try to go easy on me? Will they try to attack me? And they've been incredible." Also, a husband and dad of three, Buzzard must also balance his on-field ambitions with his family life — including a wife for 23 years who initially had some reservations about his return to the gridiron. "She told me actually a couple of weeks ago, she said, ‘I want you to make the team, but I don’t want you to play in any games,’" Buzzard recalled. "I told her those are some of the most hurtful words she’d ever told me in my life." TRAVIS KELCE INSISTS CHIEFS RETURN IN 2026 WAS NEVER IN DOUBT: 'HUNGRY TO GET BACK' Her outlook has since changed, however. Now all of her husband's games are on her calendar as she plans to cheer him on from the stands. Buzzard told NBC Bay Area that he got the idea to return to the field after his son highlighted a social media reel about a 60-year-old man playing the sport on the East Coast. To his surprise, reaching out to a coach at San Jose City College led to him lining up as a defensive end, the same position he once played years ago. For Buzzard, the comeback goes beyond football and family and into faith — something that has helped guide him through the unconventional journey. As he prays to stay healthy enough to "go the distance" and make it through the entire season, he remains eager to help his new team in every way possible. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And for anyone else wondering whether it is too late to pursue a longstanding dream, Buzzard offered a simple message: "Risk or rust. You're either risking or you're rusting as a man. Take risks. Don't rust."

articles.title: Trump’s threats anger Omanis, leave observers puzzled
articles.summary: Oman, a historic partner for the United States and proven mediator to Iran, was once again threatened by President Donald Trump over its negotiations with the Islamic Republic, leaving many in the region confused .
articles.body: Oman, a historic partner for the United States and proven mediator to Iran, was once again threatened by President Donald Trump over its negotiations with the Islamic Republic, leaving many in the region confused. Trump’s warning on Monday reiterated a threat he issued in May to “blow up” Oman over its ongoing negotiations with Iran, again concerning the Strait of Hormuz, despite Trump himself agreeing in a signed document that Muscat would “conduct dialogue” with Tehran to define the future administration and maritime services in the strait. Washington’s former ambassador to Oman, Marc J. Sievers was left “puzzled” on what caused the threats to the Gulf Arab country. “Perhaps Trump didn’t mean to be taken literally but more the matter of getting the Omani attention, which I’m sure he did,” Sievers told CNN. “It’s hard to think of Admiral Cooper planning bombing raids on Oman,” a reference to US Central Command Chief Adm. Brad Cooper. Muscat has branded itself as a neutral operator during the war, maintaining relations with Iran even as the latter fired large salvos of missiles and drones at neighboring Arab countries, and sometimes on Oman Throughout the war, it continued dialogue with Iran over ships transiting the vital Strait of Hormuz – which runs through Omani territory – and is currently negotiating with Tehran on managing the waterway despite global concern over Iran’s ambitions to seize the chokepoint. During the war, Oman allowed vessels to use its sea routes to evade the waterways precariously designated by the Revolutionary Guards. The former US top diplomat in Oman said Trump’s previous threats “upset” Oman, but Muscat “ought to see risk” in the repeated warnings. “This is the second time that President Trump has issued (a) threat. … There is obviously something behind it that you would think the Omanis would want to pay attention to,” Sievers said. It’s unclear how much progress Oman and Iran have made in their talks, or whether Washington has been involved in the ongoing negotiations – an absence that could factor into Trump’s anger toward the Gulf nation. “(Trump’s) frustration broadly stems from the fact that Muscat pursues an independent policy toward Iran that does not always align with US preferences. Ironically, however, this is precisely what enables Muscat to play the mediating role that Washington often relies upon to facilitate contact with Tehran,” Hasan Alhasan, senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told CNN. Qatar, another Gulf Arab country that has successfully mediated agreements with Iran, had coordinated its negotiations closely with the US. “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News’ Trey Yingst. Muted reaction In Oman and across the wider region, governments remained quiet and issued no condemnation or rebuke of Trump’s threats. CNN reached out to the Omani Foreign Ministry for comment but has received no response. Yet Omani social media commentators were critical of Trump’s threats. One commentator, Zakaria Al-Muharrmi, spoke about Oman’s past diplomatic assistance to the US. “America’s wise leaders know that Oman is the one that freed many detained American citizens in Tehran, and that it is the one that convinced the Houthis to stop shelling American warships, and that it is the key to the solution in the Strait of Hormuz crisis,” Al-Muharrmi wrote on X. The Omani commentator added that Trump’s “rude language” could lead to Oman freezing its efforts to save Republicans from “rising fuel bills” and an “anticipated loss in the midterm elections” Another Omani commentator, Abdullah Adawi, said that Trump chose “escalation and threats” against a US ally because it “stuck to its position and its independent decision.” Abdulkhaleq Abdullah, a political scientist from neighboring United Arab Emirates, said Trump’s threats are “completely rejected” and must be condemned by Gulf Arab countries in the “strongest terms.” ‘Misdirected and short-sighted’ An agreement intended to lead to peace talks between the US and Iran expired Monday, leaving both nations deadlocked in a stalemate over management of the Strait of Hormuz, the future of frozen Iranian funds and Tehran’s nuclear program. Both countries committed in the Memorandum of Understanding in June to achieve a “final deal in maximum 60 days” but the ceasefire was soon mired by infringements. Iran had rejected how ships were choosing to transit through the strait and began targeting vessels, and the US launched intensive strikes against Iranian targets in response. The Islamic Republic also fired missiles and drones onto neighboring countries hosting US bases. Oman and Iran are now engaged in negotiations to resolve how ships cross the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian officials. If the issue of movement in the maritime chokepoint is resolved with agreement from Washington and its allies across the region, it may remove a major hurdle towards unlocking further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions. “Trump’s anger at Oman is both misdirected and short-sighted,” Alhasan, the IISS analyst, said. “It is misdirected because Omani mediation has been sought by successive US administrations including the current one to facilitate talks with Tehran. … It is short sighted because Oman will likely be key to any future US-Iran peace deal and transit regime in the strait that emerges from it,” he said. “The US, whose strategic credibility in the region is already in shambles, cannot afford to lose a partner as critical as Oman is to the future of one of the world’s most significant and hotly contested maritime choke points.”

articles.title: Military drills between US and South Korea cut short at Washington’s request
articles.summary: The joint military drills between the United States and South Korea have been cut in half at Washington’s request, days after President Donald Trump called for their reduction, citing his close relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
articles.body: The joint military drills between the United States and South Korea have been cut in half at Washington’s request, days after President Donald Trump called for their reduction, citing his close relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise, which began on Monday, was due to run for 10 days, but will now end on Friday August 21, the militaries of both nations said. “Based on direction from the President and Secretary of War, the Department has substantially reduced Exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield while continuing training that enhances tactical capability,” a Pentagon official said. “Associated live-training events have been reduced, with certain events canceled or converted to simulations. These adjustments preserve essential readiness and training objectives,” the official said. “There will be no degradation to US training objectives.” South Korea’s military said the decision to “partially adjust the exercise period and size” of the UFS came “at the request of the US.” The revised end date comes after Trump said Sunday that he had asked Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to reduce the exercises, based on his “very good relationship” with Kim, and saying they sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. He also cited Seoul’s lack of assistance with the Iran war. South Korea has been a close American ally for over 70 years and the two nations have a mutual defense treaty, primarily designed to protect it from North Korea — a burgeoning nuclear power. But Trump’s touted personal relationship with North Korea’s Kim –– who has significantly expanded his country’s military capabilities since Trump’s first term in office and is now believed to have dozens of nuclear warheads –– has tested the long-standing partnership. While Kim himself has not commented on Trump’s call for the drills to be reduced, North Korean state media KCNA called the exercises “the most immediate and open threat” to Pyongyang and regional security in an article published Wednesday, before news broke that the exercises had been shortened. North Korea has long been critical of the annual UFS drills. Trump lamented the cost of the exercises in his Truth Social post Sunday, and said North Korea has been “unthreatening and respectful” as long as he has been president. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said he did not view Trump’s comments or order to scale back the exercises as confrontational or hostile. Seoul “sympathise(s) with President Trump’s determination and effort to create conditions for dialogue to establish peace regime on the Korean Peninsula, even if it means scaling back the recent South Korea-US joint military exercise and field training exercises,” Lee said on X Wednesday. Lee said he agrees South Korea should boost its defense spending and take responsibility for its own security in the Korean Peninsula. He added South Korea has “stated on various occasions that it will actively participate in the efforts of the international community, including the US, to restore free passage at Strait of Hormuz.” The US frequently holds joint military drills with South Korea, which hosts the largest US military installation overseas, Camp Humphreys. articles.title: Kim Jong Un’s powerful sister says she is ‘completely unaware’ if he contacted Trump
articles.summary: Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said she is “completely unaware” whether her brother communicated with US President Donald Trump, as Trump claimed this week.
articles.body: Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said she is “completely unaware” whether her brother communicated with US President Donald Trump, as Trump claimed this week. Kim, one of North Korea’s top officials, acknowledged that her brother has a “great relationship” with Trump and “personally has good memories and feelings” for him. But in a statement released on state media Wednesday, she stopped short of confirming Trump’s claim of recent contact. Trump told reporters Monday that Kim Jong Un had responded to his request for a conversation, shortly after the president demanded a sudden reduction in joint military drills with South Korea, a close and long-standing US ally. Trump did not elaborate on the contact. He added Wednesday that he intends to meet Kim later this year, but he didn’t offer details and would not say whether he has exchanged any letters with North Korea’s leader. In her statement, Kim Yo Jong said of the reported “communication” between Trump and her brother: “I am not aware of it at all, and perhaps it may be the only thing I do not know as regards the foreign policy of our supreme leadership.” Kim’s statement is illuminating because she is one of her brother’s top lieutenants and a close confidant, routinely pictured alongside the North Korean leader and someone who often delivers important statements on behalf of the often secretive and opaque rgime. Joint military drills have long irritated North Korea, and Kim Yo Jong said reducing them does not change “the provocative and offensive nature of them,” even though the US and South Korea frequently emphasize their defensive nature. Scaling the drills back should not be seen as “measure of goodwill,” Kim added. The annual joint exercises are usually scheduled to run for 10 days, but this year’s will last only five, at Washington’s request. They are designed to adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities and incorporate training to counter drones, GPS disruption and cyberattacks, a spokesperson for US Forces Korea said last week. Sudden scale down of drills Analysts have warned that by scaling down war games with South Korea, Trump risks working against his own stated goal of having Seoul assume more responsibility for its own defense. Contained within the military exercises is training to give South Korea something it hasn’t had since the Korean War began in 1950: wartime operational control of the combined South Korea-US forces on the peninsula, analysts point out. It’s a key goal for both countries. Once Seoul shows it can take on that burden, Washington can take a backseat in any future conflict, providing some firepower but letting South Korea assume most of the responsibility and cost of its defense. Trump’s demand to scale back the drills - which were months in planning - came on the first day they joint exercises began. Publicly, South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung has welcomed Trump’s request, and reiterated that he supports dialogue with North Korea and wants to take more responsibility for its own defense. “We sympathize with President Trump’s determination and effort to create conditions for dialogue to establish peace regime on the Korean Peninsula, even if it means scaling back the recent South Korea-US joint military exercise and field training exercises, and we pay tribute to that decision.” Lee said on X late Wednesday. He added he “fully agrees” with Trump that South Korea “should take responsibility itself of security on the Korean Peninsula while building sufficient capability to independently defend the peninsula by rapidly increasing defense spending to achieve a defense expenditure of 3.5% of GDP.” When calling for these exercises to be reduced, Trump cited his positive relationship with Kim Jong Un, a longtime US adversary, as well as Seoul’s lack of assistance for the war in Iran. “I get along with him,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “And you know what? The fact that I get along with him — that’s a good thing.” Trump met with Kim three times for denuclearization talks during his first term, but those talks were ultimately unsuccessful, and North Korea’s nuclear weapons program has only grown since. On Thursday, South Korea defense minister said he estimates North Korea now possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads, a range significantly higher than Trump’s recent assertion that Pyongyang has ​57 nuclear weapons. Trump took similar steps to scale back joint operations with South Korea during his first term. In March 2019, the two countries announced that their annual large-scale exercises would be reconfigured and take a reduced form. This post has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: How landscape gardening is being electrified
articles.summary: The switch to quieter electric equipment is not going as fast as some would like.
articles.body:
Part of the soundtrack to a day in southern California is the drone of petrol-powered gardening equipment.

Noise is one of the main reasons that cities around the US are banning petrol landscaping tools or encouraging electric alternatives.

These alternatives have the additional benefits of reducing carbon emissions, vibrations and the exposure of landscapers to pollution.

In addition they can mean longer working hours, as they can be used at times when residents demand quiet.

Today, I'm taking part in training run by the American Green Zone Alliance (AGZA), an organisation supporting the transition towards electric landscaping equipment.

To my surprise, the electric backpack leaf blower I strap on is not much heavier than my normal rucksack. Using the blower to herd balls around the park feels fairly intuitive, though naturally I'm much clumsier and slower than the pro landscapers.

As for noise, there's still a buzz, but the sound is higher-pitched and not quite so loud as the familiar petrol-powered machines.

The move to electric power is attracting new companies to the market for gardening kit.

US aerospace start-up Whisper Aero is one of those firms. Its main business is electric propulsion systems for aircraft.

But in 2022, after the Covid-19 pandemic made many people more sensitive to noise, and following a couple of years of research and development, the company realised that its aerospace-grade fans would work well in leaf blowers.

"Our technology is cleaner, quieter and more efficient than other air-moving technologies that exist today," according to Andrew Terajewicz, Whisper Aero's director of air management. "And the leaf blower is the perfect mix of this."

The battery on Whisper Aero's blower lasts up to 15 minutes at full power.

The company has had to scale up its manufacturing volume in its expansion to consumer technology.

Online pre-orders of Whisper Aero's handheld leaf blower started this year. It's priced at the high-end of electric leaf blowers, which are often more expensive than traditional petrol versions.

But for that you get a machine which is less likely to disturb the peace.

"It is so ultra quiet yet powerful, that the brain has a hard time understanding what's happening," says Dan Mabe, the former landscaper who founded AGZA.

Whisper Aero aims to further develop its products, including a backpack leaf blower that would be better suited to professional landscapers.

Even with innovation like that, petrol-powered machines are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, particularly for professional landscapers.

For a start, petrol machines are much more powerful, which makes for quicker work, so less time is spent lugging around heavy equipment.

Terajewicz says that heavy-duty petrol backpack blowers can reach a maximum blowing force of about 50 newtons.

The handheld Whisper Aero blower typically runs at about half that, though it can go higher.

Another big issue is runtime. Professional gardeners like to use their blowers at full throttle.

"For us, it's a little bit hard to use electric," explains Carlos Camarena, a supervisor for a California landscaping company.

Camarena's company uses electric tools where they're required to, in cities with ordinances banning petrol tools. But when they have a choice, they stick to petrol.

His company typically uses batteries that last for about 30 minutes. A crew has six batteries charging at any given time; each takes about 45 minutes to reach a full charge.

Then there's the considerable upfront cost of going electric. One landscaper estimates that it would cost his business around $10,000 (£7,540) to transition all their equipment.

The subsidies and rebates offered by some local governments may not be enough to offset the cost of the switch.

The change would be even harder for landscapers who work as sole proprietors, with a single vehicle and limited space for charging and storing equipment.

Added to that is the weight of tools with multiple batteries, and the cost of accessories to hold them all.

Nevertheless the biggest makers of power tools are investing in electric.

Stihl, a power tool manufacturer headquartered in Germany, aims for battery-powered equipment to make up 35% of its sales by next year, and 80% by 2035.

It's on track to meet the 2027 goal in Europe, though sales in the US have been slower.

To help reach its targets, the company opened its first plant solely manufacturing batteries and tools, in Romania in 2025.

"We like to say that we are dual-technology leaders," says Paul Hicks, senior marketing and product manager at Stihl GB.

"So we are being very open with our customers if in some cases a petrol tool may be a better solution for them… But in the large majority of cases, battery-power tools pay off fairly swiftly because of the cost of fuel."

In May, Stihl announced a new battery system that uses high-performance batteries.

These batteries use a relatively new, more efficient design for lithium battery cells, known as tabless cells.

Tabless cells have 60% more peak power than standard cells, according to Hicks. This means that the batteries charge faster, and landscapers can take fewer batteries out to sites.

The batteries are also relatively lightweight.

Mabe believes that overall, for gardeners embracing long-lasting electric equipment, "There's big rewards if they can make it work."

Back in southern California, landscaper Camarena sees the benefits of electric tools. "We don't contaminate the air," he says.

"When we use the gas blower, some people get mad. They are reading a book or something."

articles.title: Portugal enacts 'burqa law' largely prohibiting face coverings in public
articles.summary: Portuguese President António José Seguro has enacted a measure that bans people from covering up their face while in public places, with some exceptions, AFP reported.
articles.body: Portuguese President António José Seguro has enacted a measure that largely prohibits individuals from covering up their face while out in public, a restriction broadly viewed as being aimed at Muslim women, according to AFP. But the report noted various carve outs to the prohibition, including for health, professional, artistic, or weather-linked issues, and for when people are at locations of worship, diplomatic missions, or aboard planes. Those who fail to comply face being slapped with fines of 150 euros to 3,000 euros, according to the outlet — those figures convert to around $175 and $3,500 respectively. MS RACHEL POSTS SUPPORT FOR HIJAB-WEARING KINDERGARTNERS AFTER TRUMP POST The final edition of the measure, which has been characterized by local media as the "burqa law" in reference to the body and face covering that some Muslim women wear, was adopted by the Portuguese parliament last month, according to AFP. The law bans sporting coverings meant to hide a person's face or block identification in public areas, and bans requiring someone to cloak their face due to gender, religion, age, or origin, the report states. EL-SAYED BOOKED FOR MAJOR ISLAMIC CONVENTION ALONGSIDE CLERICS WITH RADICAL PASTS "For the President of the Republic, the uncovered face constitutes a structuring dimension of social trust, a characteristic of Portuguese society," according to an English translation of a Portuguese-language press release. "Social integration, non-discrimination based on gender, and the security resulting from similar decisions by the European Court of Human Rights underpin this decision. The President of the Republic shares this Court's conviction that the face is central to human identity and communication, serving as a minimum element for mutual recognition among fellow citizens," the release notes. articles.title: ‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
articles.summary: From father searching for his daughter’s body to man who drowned trying to save a friend, floods take devastating toll.
articles.body:
Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neighbouring Nagaland state where he worked.

But when his phone rang at about 11am on July 19, there was panic in the voice of his 30-year-old wife, Dipika.

list 2 of 3 On huge river island in India’s Assam, annual floods threaten local arts

list 3 of 3 ‘Nowhere else to go’: In India’s Assam, frequent floods hit river islanders

“I could only see my wife telling me on the video call, ‘This is it for us. We are going to die,’ before the call was disconnected,” Panika recalled, speaking to Al Jazeera.

It was the last time they spoke. Moments later, rising waters from the nearby Dikhow River, which snakes past their village in Assam’s Sivasagar district, surged into their bamboo-and-mud home with a ferocious current and swept away Dipika and four-year-old daughter Radhika.

“The water came flooding like sea waves, and they were gone in a flash,” Panika said, as he stood in front of the ruined home he has since returned to.

Sivasagar is part of the eastern Assam region, also referred to as Upper Assam. Incessant rains between July 18 and July 20 submerged the region and the neighbouring Naga Hills of Nagaland.

Monsoon floods usually impact northern and western Assam, and parts of central Assam, the worst. But several Nagaland districts bordering Upper Assam received heavy rainfall on those three days, leading to dozens of landslides. This intense run-off swelled Naga Hills-origin rivers and caused devastation downstream.

The resultant floods killed more than 100 people, destroyed 2,700 villages, and displaced 700,000 people across the state. The state government says 1.2 million people were impacted in all, their lives disrupted.

Most waters have since receded, but Radhika’s body is yet to be found.

“I look for Radhika every day in the bushes, tirelessly,” Panika said, holding back his tears. “Her last words, calling me ‘Papa’, are still reverberating in my ears.”

Panika’s other daughter, Ridhika, 10, was at a relative’s place a few metres away when her mother and sister were swept away by the flood. Ridhika held onto a bamboo bush and was later rescued by locals.

Several riverine villages in Sivasagar have been wrecked by debris carried down by the waters of the Dikhow from the surrounding Naga Hills.

Tens of thousands of tree trunks lie piled up in places that used to be homes, as lush rice fields, the main source of livelihood, have been washed away.

Kukil Das, a 30-year-old Facebook vlogger in Debiram’s village of Nepali Khuti, told Al Jazeera that “the torrent of the flood was like an apocalyptic event seen in the movies.

“Trees as tall as 30 to 40 metres (100-130ft) came down from the hills, flooding the river, and wiped out everything as they crashed against our homes,” he said. “There is no home left. It was a tsunami.”

Das and his friend Shravan Prasad, from the neighbouring Bihubor village, said they saved at least 1,000 lives by using boats the two villages had at that time.

“We put together a group of friends with the seven boats and started rescuing people turn by turn for two days and nights without food and water,” Prasad said.

Das said the floods forced residents to take shelter on the roofs of concrete homes they could find, as cries for help and the sounds of the river washing away homes echoed in the neighbourhood.

Laxmi Sharma, who owned one such concrete house, said she provided shelter to at least 60 people on her terrace after the river water gushed into Nepali Khuti.

“People ran towards the roof of my building. We thought we were going to die,” Sharma, 46, told Al Jazeera. “But it is a miracle that we are still alive even though my house was barely out of water.”

Not everyone could escape the flood’s wrath, though.

In Sivasagar’s Simaluguri village, two friends – Reihana Ahmed, a Muslim, and Ratul Swarna, a Hindu, both in their 30s – were swept away in the torrent.

When Ahmed, a mother of two, was drowning as the deluge entered her village, Swarna, who did not know how to swim, jumped to save her without thinking about his life.

The two friends were later found dead in the paddy fields. “It was humanity that won in a disaster like this,” Ahmed’s husband Aminul Haque said with a sorrowful smile.

Besides the eroding banks of the Dikhow River in Prajabasti, another flood-affected village, 75-year-old Asor Ali sat in disbelief next to his wife, Jamila Khatun.

“Even the generations preceding me have not seen a flood like this,” he said, staring at the flowing river. “Even the 1950s earthquake that triggered the floods here did not do so much damage.”

A magnitude 8.6 earthquake hit Assam and Tibet across the border in 1950, altering the region’s riverine system. Nearly 5,000 people died. Since then, Assam has witnessed frequent floods, which intensify during the monsoons, says Mirza Zulfiqur Rahman, a researcher on the basin of the Brahmaputra, the region’s major river: The Naga Hills rivers that flooded Upper Assam are its tributaries.

But residents say this year’s deadly deluge is not just a natural phenomenon.

Biren Gogoi, 43, says rampant stone and sand mining in regional rivers, coupled with aggressive deforestation and coal extraction in Nagaland’s Mon district, triggered the devastation.

Global Nature Watch, an open-source online platform that provides real-time data on deforestation across the world, showed that Nagaland lost 14 percent of its tree cover between 2002 and 2025, with Mon district bordering Assam’s Sivasagar being the most affected.

According to the latest report published in 2023 by the Forest Survey of India, Nagaland has lost about 794.88 square kilometres (306.9 square miles) of forest cover between 2013 and 2023.

Al Jazeera travelled along the Assam-Nagaland border and saw signs of deforestation on the hills and mining activities in both the states. Satellite images also confirmed rampant coal mining in Nagaland’s Mon district, and stone mining crushers on Assam’s side, especially in Bihubor, one of the epicentres of the Assam flood.

While Mon’s Deputy Commissioner Wennyei Konyak acknowledged the possibility of illegal mining in the district, he added that the land was protected under Indian laws to uphold the rights of Indigenous tribes, and therefore government interference in the area was limited.

“I would not blame mining activities for the flood. It was just the wrath of nature,” he told Al Jazeera.

But experts and political leaders in Assam say mining played a direct role in the floods.

Debabrata Saikia of the opposition Congress party, who is a former legislator from Sivasagar constituency, accused Assam’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of allowing illegal excavations for stone and sand on the Dikhow riverbank, resulting in a cratered wasteland that worsened the floods.

“This unchecked plundering of riverbeds and hills under the ruling government has engineered this into a man-made disaster,” Saikia told Al Jazeera.

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, however, rejected the allegation on August 4, blaming excessive rainfall in Nagaland for triggering the Upper Assam deluge. On August 14, Ranoj Pegu, a cabinet minister in the state’s BJP government, blamed erratic rainfall due to climate change for the deluge.

Rahman, the Brahmaputra river basin researcher, believes that while the climate crisis played a role, the flood was “purely human-made”, caused by the fracturing of the landscape.

“The unrestrained stone extraction from the Dikhow riverbed has damaged the river’s natural cushion,” Rahman said. “That means the river loses the capacity to resist high flows of torrents that break embankments and cause floods.”

An official document from 2022, seen by Al Jazeera, also highlights mining as a factor in possible large-scale floods downstream on the Assam side.

Al Jazeera reached out to senior district officials in Sivasagar as well as state government officials for their comments on allegations of unchecked coal mining but did not get any response.

Back in Prajabasti village, Ali, the septuagenarian, is mentally preparing himself for future floods.

“It will happen again, so long as there is greed for land and coal in humans,” he said. “Nature pays them back.”

articles.title: Sri Lankan cricket legend Kumar Sangakkara spent years restoring a historic villa built more than 100 years ago, blending old-world architecture with modern design; the heritage property is now ready for a new chapter
articles.summary: Kumar Sangakkara is a name that needs no introduction. Everyone who follows cricket or even who doesnât, knows the Sri Lankan cricket legend. But what.
articles.body: Kumar Sangakkara is a name that needs no introduction. Everyone who follows cricket or even who doesnât, knows the Sri Lankan cricket legend. But what people donât know is that back in 2008, Kumar Sangakkara along with his wife Yehali bought a house inside Galle Fort, also known as the Dutch Fort or the "Ramparts of Galle". The couple were already in love with its scenic coastal location, but were not aware of what was inside the fort. When they bought the 120-year old villa, their first look came with an unpleasant surprise because it was in such poor condition.But 20 years later, the property has emerged as an unusual meeting point of Sri Lankaâs history and modern design. Itâs a restoration that recently took the world by surprise after featuring by ABC Australiaâs Culture by Design.However, for travellers the story is about more than a famous cricketerâs beautiful home. It offers a glimpse into why Galle Fort is among Sri Lankaâs most fascinating heritage destinations. Why restoring a historic building is very different from simply renovating an old house.Letâs find out more about the iconic propertyA home inside one of Asiaâs great fortified citiesGalle Fort is set on Sri Lankaâs southwestern coast. It has also been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988. UNESCO describes the Old Town of Galle and its fortifications as an outstanding example of a European-built fortified city in South and Southeast Asia.The story of the fort goes back to the 16th century. It was the time the Portuguese established the fortified settlement, and under Dutch rule in the 17th and 18th centuries, the fort developed into the remarkable place that visitors see today. Later British influence added another layer to the region.This incredible mix is exactly what makes walking through Galle Fort so atmospheric. Narrow streets, verandas, courtyards, old houses, churches, warehouses and massive ramparts sit alongside cafÃ©s, galleries, shops and homes.Sri Lanka Tourism describes Galle Fort as a historical, archaeological and architectural monument with 14 major bastions, while UNESCO highlights its distinctive street grid, courtyards, verandas and even a 17th-century underground drainage system that remains in use.Sangakkaraâs dreamFor Sangakkara and Yehali, the main challenge was to retain the fortâs old look without stripping off its identity. They called in architects Jeevan D'Souza and Murad Ismail and interior designer Annika Fernando to make their dream into reality. Rather than treating the historic fabric as something that needed to be hidden behind freshly finished surfaces, the team chose to make much of it part of the design.Some of the villa's old coral construction was deliberately left exposed including weathered walls and layers of patina. Talking to ABC, Fernando said that the contrast between aged surfaces and clean new finishes eventually became an important part of the home's character.A unique design challengeOne of the most memorable details from the restoration involves a huge sculpture by Sri Lankan artist Prageeth Manohansa.The sculpture was intended to become a centrepiece of the home, but there was a problem: it was too big to pass through any of the doors. But the problemâs solution was wonderfully unconventional. The artwork was brought into the house before the restoration began, and the building was then renovated around it.It is a small detail, but it captures the philosophy behind the project. Instead of forcing the historic house to conform completely to modern requirements, the designers repeatedly worked around what was already there.From damaged villa to modern family homeToday, itâs a four-bedroom residence with three courtyard gardens and a rooftop swimming pool overlooking the historic surroundings, including views towards Galle Lighthouse. Rooms combine contemporary interiors with artworks, antiques and surviving elements of the original building.Sangakkara described the house as a reflection of how new residents coexist with an old community. That idea matters in Galle Fort, which is not merely an archaeological site but a living historic urban area. UNESCO's current conservation guidance specifically encourages restoration and adaptive reuse while stressing the importance of retaining historically authentic building fabric.Galle Fort, a must-visit attraction in Sri LankaFor travellers, Sangakkara's villa is a reminder to look beyond the postcard views of Galle Fort.Walk along the ramparts around sunset, explore the narrow lanes, notice the old verandas and courtyards, visit the historic churches and museums, and look closely at how different architectural traditions overlap.It is the country's one of the most distinctive attractions, while UNESCO's World Heritage designation rests on precisely this unusual interaction between European architecture and South Asian traditions.Sangakkara's restoration adds another chapter to that story. His villa demonstrates that conservation does not necessarily mean turning a historic building into a relic. Sometimes, the best way to preserve a building is to give it another lifeâcarefully, respectfully and without hiding the marks of time.Inside this particular Galle Fort house, the old still live, the courtyards have been revived and modern life has moved in but the old is gold character can still be felt. The cricket legend may have traded the stadium for a heritage villa, but his most interesting Galle project is ultimately a lesson in travel itself.For visitors, it also offers a different way to experience heritage: not simply by photographing old walls, but by understanding the stories, craftsmanship and lives that continue to shape them today. For anyone planning a trip to Sri Lanka, Galle Fort is therefore worth experiencing slowly rather than treating it as a quick sightseeing stop. Its real charm lies in the details. An old doorway, a weathered wall, a shaded courtyard or a house that has been given a new purpose without losing its pastSources: ABC Australiaâs Culture by Design; UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Sri Lanka Tourism; UNESCO state-of-conservation and heritage documentation.Looking for trusted parenting advice?
